pests.name: Cabbageworms, loopers, and diamondback moths
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see ragged holes chewed in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and dark droppings, and worst of all, caterpillars and their mess tucked down into the curd, where they are very hard to wash out.
pests.cause_beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants, chew the leaves, and crawl into the head you want to eat.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray Bt, which is low in toxicity to people, pets and bees and acts on caterpillars rather than on insects in general, or spinosad. Bt cannot tell a pest caterpillar from a butterfly one, so treat only the plants that have a problem. Pick caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs, clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in the leaves with green caterpillars and dark frass; as the curd forms, larvae crawl into it and foul it, the costly damage that is very hard to clean from a tight white curd. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed (Clemson rates the diamondback the most numerous cole-crop caterpillar in home gardens).
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage and contaminate the curd; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Cauliflower is a primary host for all three.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad, which target caterpillars and spare beneficials, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down. Tighten control as the curd forms, when contamination of the head is the expensive kind.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use floating row cover or fine mesh from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

pests.name: Cabbage aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and tucked into the curd, where they are very hard to wash out. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
pests.cause_beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast. They love cabbage-family plants and hide down in the curd, which is the part you eat.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, which eat aphids.
pests.prevention_beginner: Check the growing tips and the developing curd often and act early. Go easy on nitrogen once the curd forms, since soft growth draws them, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid forms dense colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides and then lodges in the curd, where it contaminates the marketable product with insects and honeydew and is nearly impossible to clean from the tight florets. Curling and distortion of young leaves is common.
pests.cause_seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid, sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; contamination of the harvested curd with aphids and sticky honeydew is usually the real problem rather than plant stunting. Pressure is heaviest on the long-season fall crop.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (the parasitoid Diaeretiella rapae, hoverflies, ladybugs) that suppress this aphid.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout growing tips and the curd weekly and catch infestations before aphids colonize the head. Avoid excess nitrogen once the curd sets, use row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

pests.name: Cabbage root maggot
pests.symptoms_beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet soil.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp weather, so spring transplants are most at risk.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at spring establishment, and a root-checked plant is also far likelier to button.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly (Delia radicum) tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants and opening the door to rots.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

pests.name: Harlequin bug
pests.symptoms_beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
pests.cause_beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped eggs laid in rows, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region brassica specialist.
pests.cause_seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a true bug that specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes several generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap, pyrethrum, or neem help where pressure is severe.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover, and a stunted cauliflower seedling often heads early and badly.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle the damage.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts or kills seedlings and slows establishment, and a checked cauliflower seedling is prone to buttoning.
pests.cause_seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas and are most damaging at the seedling stage; a vigorous transplant generally outgrows them, but a stalled seedling can be set back badly.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage without a growth check.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
diseases.cause_beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil from being too acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Don't grow cauliflower or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots. A clubroot-checked plant rarely makes a usable curd.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and infects most readily in acidic soils below pH 6.5.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (UMN advises up to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

diseases.name: Black rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot the curd.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and rot the curd. Often the most serious cole-crop disease in warm, wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants (a hot-water seed treatment helps), rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

diseases.name: Alternaria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small dark spots with rings like a target appear on the leaves and can spread onto the curd as brown, fuzzy patches that ruin it. It is worse in warm, wet weather.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads by spores in wet weather and on infected seed. It spots the leaves and, on cauliflower, can blemish the white curd, which makes it unsellable.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove badly spotted leaves, improve airflow so leaves dry, and use a copper spray if it is spreading onto the curd. Keep water off the leaves.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with clean seed, space plants for airflow, water at the soil rather than overhead, rotate away from cabbage-family crops, and clear away old plants where the fungus survives.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small dark leaf spots with concentric target-like rings and a yellow halo; in wet weather the spots enlarge, and on cauliflower the fungus can spread onto the curd as a brown, sometimes fuzzy discoloration that ruins its market quality. Clemson lists Alternaria brown spot among the main cauliflower diseases.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria species (A. brassicae / A. brassicicola), fungi that spread by airborne and splashed spores and on infected seed; long leaf wetness and warm, humid weather favor them, and they survive in crop debris and on seed.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves, improve airflow and let foliage dry, and apply a copper-based fungicide if the disease threatens the curd; control is largely preventive.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean, certified, hot-water-treated seed, space for airflow, water at the soil line, rotate away from brassicas, and bury or remove crop debris that carries the fungus over.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves and can spot the curd.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors the leaves and can spot and darken the curd. Cauliflower's cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora parasitica) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

diseases.name: Bacterial soft rot (head rot)
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The curd develops soft, watery, brown or black mushy patches that quickly turn slimy and smell bad. It usually shows up in warm, wet weather on a curd that stayed wet.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria get into the curd through small wounds or where water sits in the head, then rot it from the inside, especially in warm, humid weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure for a rotting curd, so remove affected heads. The fix is prevention: keep the curd dry and harvest promptly.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep water off the curd, give plants room so heads dry quickly after rain, blanch (tie the leaves) loosely so water doesn't pool, harvest promptly, and avoid bruising the heads.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, water-soaked brown to black lesions on the curd that rapidly become slimy and foul-smelling, the bacterial head rot Clemson lists for cauliflower; it spreads fastest in warm, wet weather and where water sits in a tied (blanched) head.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soft-rot bacteria (Pectobacterium / Pseudomonas species) enter through wounds and natural openings and macerate the curd tissue; free moisture in the head and warm, humid conditions drive it, and a tightly tied blanch that traps water raises the risk.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for a rotting curd; remove and discard affected heads. Management is cultural and preventive.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Keep the curd dry: space for airflow, blanch loosely so water drains rather than pools, avoid overhead watering and handling wet heads, harvest promptly once the curd is full, and do not bruise the heads.
